articleSummary: Robert Koch, a German physician and microbiologist, discovered Bacillus anthracis as the cause of anthrax in 1876, providing the first demonstration that a specific microbe causes a specific disease. On 24 March 1882, he identified the Mycobacterium tuberculosis as the causative agent of tuberculosis, a landmark in infectious disease control. In 1883, during expeditions to Egypt and India, he identified Vibrio cholerae as the causative agent of cholera, informing water- and sanitation-related public health measures. He formulated the four fundamental postulates of bacteriology, linking microbes to disease. Koch founded the Royal Prussian Institute for Infectious Diseases in Berlin (now the Robert Koch Institute) and earned the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. Arriving at Brioni in 1900 at Paul Kupelwieser’s invitation, he studied endemic malaria, directing marsh drainage to reduce mosquito populations; Brioni then became a center for malaria training in Croatia. He died in 1910 in Germany, remembered as a pioneering 19th-century physician.

articleHeadline: Mathematical modeling of sequential Dengue-Zika infections: dynamic insights into antibody-dependent enhancement and neutralization effects - Scientific Reports
articleSummary: Dengue and Zika sequential infections are modeled to probe antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) and neutralization in a human–vector framework. Global dynamics depend on parameters that govern transmission and recovery: mosquito biting rate e, transmission probabilities (human–vector and vector–human), and recovery rates. Surface plots illustrate that higher e and transmission probabilities raise the basic reproduction number and endemic infection levels, while higher recovery mitigates risk, with interactions potentially driving R0 toward ~4.85 in certain scenarios.

articleSummary: TB remains one of the deadliest global infectious diseases. In 2024, TB caused about 1.23 million deaths, including 150,000 among people living with HIV, with an estimated 10.7 million new cases across all ages and countries. The WHO issued new guidelines promoting near-patient, portable diagnostic devices and novel sampling methods, such as tongue swabs and combined sputum testing, to shorten diagnosis and accelerate treatment, with results in about one hour. These tools offer multi-disease detection potential for HIV, monkeypox, and HPV and support more patient-centered, integrated care. Yet funding constraints and limited uptake threaten progress; costs and dependence on centralized labs reduce access. The agency urges bedside urine tests and other validated approaches to speed diagnosis. World TB Day 2026 theme: "Yes, we can end TB: government empowerment, collective action." China’s experience highlights rural-urban coverage, volunteer networks, and youth engagement.

articleSummary: Bronze Age Yersinia pestis DNA was found in a domesticated sheep from Arkaim in the southern Ural Mountains, linking the 4,000-year-old plague to the same lineage that infected people across Eurasia. Lacking the flea-survival gene, Bronze Age plague could not rely on the rat–flea–human chain seen in the 14th‑century Black Death, which killed about one-third of Europe. Researchers propose livestock as a bridge between wild reservoirs and humans, with rodents remaining the strongest candidate reservoir, though migratory birds may have aided long-distance movement. In a screen of 23 animal remains from Arkaim, only one sheep yielded plague DNA, yet enough of the genome survived to place it in the ancient plague lineage. The finding highlights zoonosis and suggests that as herding and trade expanded, spillovers from animal hosts fueled human infections. More bones from animals and humans may reveal whether this was rare or routine.

articleHeadline: CDC issues global travel notice as dengue fever reaches Americas
articleSummary: On 2026-03-24, the CDC issued a Level 1 global travel advisory for dengue fever amid spiraling outbreaks worldwide. articleSummary: Taiwan’s 2025 TB data show incidence at 25 per 100,000 with 5,742 new cases, a 66% drop from 73 per 100,000 in 2005, and the first-time fall below 6,000 cases. Long-term targets aim for 2030 incidence of 10 per 100,000 and 2035 TB elimination. About two-thirds of new cases occur in the elderly; 65+ patients predominate, with 85+ accounting for over 15% of the elderly group. Early TB symptoms are often non-specific; cough >2 weeks, chest pain, weight loss, fever, and poor appetite warrant prompt medical attention. The program will expand latent TB infection screening and treatment in long-term care facilities and among diabetes and dialysis patients. Foreign-born individuals comprise ~10% of cases (mainly from Vietnam, Thailand, Indonesia), totaling ~700–800 new cases annually; government funds ~NT$800 million this year for migrant screening and publicly funded treatment. Short-course DOTS therapy already yields 85–90% treatment completion, with potential 10–15% further gains.

articleSummary: Tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) remains a major global health crisis, causing about 1.2 million deaths per year, with rising drug resistance in the Asia-Pacific region. By targeting this complex, the compounds disrupt protein homeostasis and impair bacterial viability. The study, published in Nature Communications, traced changes across more than 3,000 Mycobacterium tuberculosis proteins, highlighting how interrupting a single essential complex can remodel the bacterial proteome.
